name: Karao
confidence_why: Brainard 1994, the only phonological description of Karao, states that stress is non-contrastive and predictable but falls freely on the final or penultimate syllable of words spoken in isolation and shifts with clitics, with the exact rules not yet worked out, and no other source addresses Karao stress.
catalog_citation: Brainard, Sherri. 1994. The phonology of Karao, the Philippines. Pacific Linguistics B-110. Canberra: Australian National University.

catalog_quote: Phonological stress in Karao has not been fully analysed ... Secondly, there is evidence that stress is not contrastive, but predictable in Karao, although the exact rules for assigning stress appear to be complex. There are a number of empirical facts that point to this hypothesis: (a) There are no minimal pairs or near minimal pairs of words that contrast in stress only. (b) When a freestanding morpheme is pronounced in isolation, phonological stress can occur freely on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable; for example, the freestanding noun [ŋařan] 'name' may be pronounced ['ŋařan] or [ŋa'řan]. If stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word, it can be maintained in that position by shifting one syllable to the right when one-syllable suffixes and enclitics are added to the word. ... sources.citation: Himes, Ronald S. 1998. The Southern Cordilleran group of Philippine languages. Oceanic Linguistics 37(1): 120-177.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 122: "At some point in the development of the current SC languages, phonemic vowel length was lost, and stress became predictable. Under most circumstances, the first syllable of a word took on stress if that syllable was open and had a vowel other than *i [barred i]. ... It is also likely that, during this same PSC time period, stress fell on the last vowel of a word if that vowel was preceded by a high vowel and its corresponding glide." p. 125 (sec. 2.2.1, stated for all Nuclear SC languages, which per Table 1 p. 121 are Ibaloy, Kalanguya and Karaw): "As in all of the NuSC languages stress falls predictably on the first syllable of a word whose shape is CV.CV(C) unless that syllable has a reflex of *i [barred i]. In the latter event, stress remains on the second syllable." p. 129 (sec. 2.3 Karaw): "This variation is dealt with here in terms of stress, syllable position, and the quality of the preceding vowel." Karaw examples with stress marked: *tilu > tAdo/tado 'three', *sigip > sAkAp/sakAp 'below', *timuk > tAmok/tamok 'forehead' (final stress, first-syllable vowel a reflex of *i) p. 129; *?ubi > ?ugi 'yam', *mata > matha 'eye', *kuku > koxo 'fingernail' p. 130; pAxow 'ches
sources.locator: pp. 122 (PSC/SC general stress statement), 125 (NuSC rule, sec. 2.2.1), 129-131 (sec. 2.3 Karaw, examples with stress marks), 159 (irregular-stress note)
sources.note: Comparative study of Southern Cordilleran (Ibaloi, Kallahan, Karao, Pangasinan, Ilongot); may comment on whether Karao retains the contrastive Philippine accent found in relatives (bears on our 'non-contrastive, variable within final two syllables' coding). Comparative, not descriptive; low priority.
